feed.title: VanoForum
feed.subtitle: Guides, sheets and tools for researchers

entry.title: Focus, rest and the unconscious work of research
entry.summary: Hard problems are solved in alternation. Concentrated work, then a step back while the mind keeps working, then new insight. Protect deep focus, accept that your time is finite, use breaks deliberately, and sleep on hard problems.

entry.title: Impostor feelings in research
entry.summary: Many researchers feel they are frauds who will soon be found out, despite clear evidence of their competence. The feeling is common, it is not a diagnosis, and it can be managed. Separate feelings from evidence, keep a record of what you have done, and talk about it.

entry.title: Mental health during the PhD
entry.summary: Depression and anxiety are common among doctoral students, and much of the risk comes from how the work is organised. Know the evidence, recognise the warning signs early, protect what helps, and ask for help before things become serious.

entry.title: Thinking on paper: research notebooks
entry.summary: Published papers hide how research was done. Notebooks keep it. From Newton's Waste Book to Faraday's numbered diaries, the great experimenters thought on paper. Here is what they did, and a simple notebook practice for your own research.

entry.title: Science is a strong-link problem
entry.summary: In some problems the worst parts decide the outcome. In others only the best parts matter. Science is mostly of the second kind, and seeing it that way changes how to choose problems, how to judge others' work and how to spend a career.

entry.title: Are our best theories true?
entry.summary: Scientific theories predict with astonishing precision, yet history is full of successful theories that turned out false. Structural realism offers a way out. Theories may be wrong about what exists and still right about the mathematical structure of the world.

entry.title: How science justifies its claims
entry.summary: Falsification is the scientist's favourite philosophy, but it is not how science works. Theories are tested together with assumptions, supported by evidence in degrees, and replaced in long programmes. Mathematics adds its own path, from examples and conjectures to proofs.

entry.title: Building an academic career
entry.summary: Few doctoral graduates obtain a permanent academic position. Hiring committees decide on evidence, not potential. Know what evidence they look for, finish your projects, plan for the gaps in your record, and decide consciously whether to play.

entry.title: What older papers teach about writing
entry.summary: Papers written a century ago were often easier to read than today's. Keep the precision of modern writing, and take back what older papers did well. Say why you did the work, give one main idea, and state honestly what you do not know.

entry.title: Understanding peer review
entry.summary: What peer review is for, where it comes from, what it does well and what it does not. Knowing its limits helps you write papers that pass it, read reports calmly, and review fairly yourself.

entry.title: Skimming a paper in twenty minutes
entry.summary: You cannot read every paper in full. Read the few paragraphs that carry the story, then the figures and the topic sentences, and decide in twenty minutes whether a paper deserves a deep reading.

entry.title: Getting better at research
entry.summary: Research is a set of skills that can be trained. Choose your own problems, train your taste by making predictions, read beyond the trending papers, write everything down, shorten the loop between idea and test, and find people who tell you the truth.

entry.title: What a PhD expects from you
entry.summary: The unwritten rules of the doctorate. Own your project, bring questions rather than answers, ask whether a problem is worth solving, and make every expectation with your supervisor explicit.

entry.title: Writing the thesis
entry.summary: How to turn your papers and notes into a coherent thesis. Structure, the general introduction, chapters built from papers, writing schedule, working with the committee, and preparing the defence.

entry.title: Managing your PhD
entry.summary: A year-by-year plan for the doctorate, how to work with your supervisor, keep a research journal, handle being stuck, protect your health, and finish on time.

entry.title: Conferences and networking
entry.summary: How to choose conferences, apply for travel funding, prepare a short talk or poster, talk to senior researchers, and turn meetings into lasting professional relationships.

entry.title: Collaboration and authorship
entry.summary: How to start and run a research collaboration, share work fairly, decide author order, and avoid the most common conflicts. Includes the conventions of mathematics and other fields.

entry.title: Writing a literature review
entry.summary: How to search the literature systematically, organise what you read, and write a review that compares ideas instead of listing papers. Useful for a thesis chapter, a survey or the background section of a paper.

entry.title: Giving a research talk
entry.summary: How to plan, build and deliver a research talk. Know the audience, follow the three-part structure, design clear slides or board work, rehearse, and handle questions.

entry.title: Posting a preprint on arXiv
entry.summary: How to prepare, submit and update a preprint on arXiv. Accounts and endorsement, choosing categories, licences, TeX source, versions, and the link with journal submission.

entry.title: The academic phrasebook
entry.summary: Reusable English phrases for every part of a research paper, sorted by function. Announcing results, defining, comparing with earlier work, structuring proofs, hedging, and concluding.

entry.title: Becoming a good scientific writer
entry.summary: Good writing is a habit, not a talent. Read for style, keep a phrasebook, write every day, get feedback, and revise in passes. A practical training plan for researchers who write in a second language.

entry.title: Applying for postdoctoral positions
entry.summary: The postdoc job market runs on a yearly calendar. Where positions are posted, what goes in the research statement, how to manage letters, and how to compare offers.

entry.title: Funding your PhD and finding scholarships
entry.summary: Never start a PhD without funding. The kinds of funding that exist, the main national and international programmes, and how to make a scholarship application stand out.

entry.title: The PhD application file
entry.summary: The academic CV, the statement of purpose, the research proposal, the letters of recommendation and the interview. What each document is for, and how to make it specific.

entry.title: Choosing a supervisor
entry.summary: The supervisor matters more than the university name. What to look for, the questions to ask, how to talk to current students, and the warning signs to take seriously.

entry.title: Contacting a professor
entry.summary: How to write the first email to a potential supervisor or collaborator, what to attach, when to follow up, and the mistakes that send an email straight to the archive.

entry.title: Finding a PhD abroad
entry.summary: How doctoral admission works in the main systems, where funded positions are advertised, and a twelve-month plan from the first search to the first day in a new country.

entry.title: A research method, from the first idea to the preprint
entry.summary: Choosing a problem, working in examples, discussing the strategy before writing proofs, checking originality, keeping a research log, and writing to other researchers about their work.

entry.title: Submission, cover letters and peer review
entry.summary: What to check before submitting, how to write a short cover letter, what happens during review, and how to answer referees point by point. Also how to write a referee report yourself.

entry.title: Choosing a journal
entry.summary: Scope first, then level, then the editor. What Q1 and Q2 really mean, how to read an editorial board, how to recognize a predatory journal, and how to build a realistic list of targets.

entry.title: Revising paragraphs, step by step
entry.summary: A method to revise a paragraph without losing your voice. Check the content first, then the structure, then the sentences, then the words. Keep your notation and your structure intact.

entry.title: Presenting results and proofs
entry.summary: How to organize sections, choose between Theorem, Proposition and Lemma, write proofs that read as prose, display equations, and keep the LaTeX source clean.

entry.title: Writing the introduction, the motivation and the contribution
entry.summary: An introduction tells a short story. Where the problem comes from, why it matters, what was missing, and what this paper adds, with the main results stated early and the proofs kept for later.

entry.title: Writing the abstract
entry.summary: An abstract is a short, exact advertisement for the paper. Start with what you prove, give every main contribution, use strong verbs, and leave the symbols out.

entry.title: Writing your first paper in English
entry.summary: The anatomy of a research paper, the order in which to write it, and the sentence-level habits that make English academic prose clear, even when English is not your first language.

entry.title: Tools for finding, reading and managing papers
entry.summary: Where to search, how to follow new work, how to read PDFs efficiently and how to keep a library you can still use in five years.

entry.title: How to read a research paper
entry.summary: A three-pass method, a map of the results, and a one-page reading sheet. Read for what the paper proves and how, not line by line from page one.
